SUMMARY: FRENCH WINDSTORM NILS CAUSES €586M IN INSURED LOSSES

In mid-February, extratropical windstorm Nils (also called Ulrike) hit southwest France's Nouvelle-Aquitaine and Occitanie regions, generating approximately €586 million in insured losses according to PERILS, a catastrophe data aggregator.

THE STORM'S IMPACT

Between February 11-13, Nils delivered damaging winds and heavy rainfall onto already-saturated ground. France had experienced its wettest start to a year on record since 1959, which amplified flooding risks. The Garonne, Dordogne, and Charente river basins flooded, while the Alps faced exceptional avalanche danger.

At peak intensity, the storm knocked out electricity for 900,000 households and disrupted transportation. Physical damage was widespread: thousands of homes suffered roof damage, light structures were destroyed, and structural wind damage drove most of the insured losses.

WHY THIS MATTERS

The €586 million figure covers property and motor insurance claims. While this represents a significant hit to the French insurance market, it's notably smaller than Windstorm Klaus from January 2009, which caused €1.574 billion in losses. Klaus had more intense wind gusts. Nils arrived just over a month after Windstorm Goretti, which also substantially impacted France, suggesting the region faces increasing storm frequency.

TECHNICAL NOTES

PERILS classified Nils as a windstorm rather than a flood event because wind caused the majority of losses. A subsequent storm called Pedro hit the region a week later but fell outside the standard 72-hour reinsurance definition window, so it's counted separately. PERILS will issue a revised loss estimate on May 13, 2026, three months post-event.

INSURANCE INDUSTRY BRIEFING: AON EXPANDS STORM LOSS TRACKING SERVICE

THE CORE ISSUE

Severe convective storms (basically organized clusters of thunderstorms that produce hail, tornadoes, and heavy wind) have quietly become the insurance industry's biggest problem. In 2025, these storms generated 61 billion dollars in global insured losses, with 52 billion of that coming from the US alone. This isn't a one-time hurricane event - it's recurring, spreading across seasons, and catching the industry off-guard.

WHY THIS MATTERS

Insurance companies operate on razor-thin margins. They need to know quickly how much money they're about to lose when a major event happens, because that affects everything: whether they need to tap reinsurance agreements, how to deploy claims adjusters, whether to suspend new policies in affected areas, and ultimately their quarterly earnings. The faster and more accurate that loss estimate, the better decisions they make.

THE SOLUTION

Aon, a major broker that sits between insurance companies and reinsurers, has upgraded its Automated Event Response service to track US severe convective storms. Think of it as a real-time loss calculator during and immediately after storms.

The service combines three inputs: Aon's own catastrophe modeling, daily weather data, and actual storm reports. Once a storm system develops, it generates updated loss estimates every day for 72 hours after the event ends. Crucially, it breaks down losses by how each insurer is exposed - their gross position, their reinsured portion, and their net exposure.

THE PRACTICAL ANGLE

This addresses a genuine pain point. During an active storm event, insurers face enormous uncertainty. They don't know if the system will intensify, stall, or move north. They don't know yet how many claims they'll receive or how severe they'll be. But they do need to make decisions - right now - about capital deployment and reinsurance triggers. Better daily estimates reduce that uncertainty window.

The service also helps with communication. Insurers can tell reinsurers and investors "here's what we're seeing today" with reasonable confidence, rather than issuing wildly varying estimates as information comes in.

RELEVANCE BEYOND INSURANCE

The catastrophe bond market cares about this too. Many catastrophe bonds cover severe convective storm exposure, and bond investors need the same real-time loss intelligence that insurers do. Better data means less panic selling in that market during active events.

THE BIGGER PICTURE

This reflects a shift in how the insurance industry thinks about tail risk. Hurricanes are still catastrophic, but they're rare and well-understood. Severe convective storms are becoming the normalized volatility that eats away at profitability year after year. Tools like this represent the industry adapting to a new baseline of chaos.

REINSURANCE SECTOR FACING STRUCTURAL SHIFT TOWARD ALTERNATIVE CAPITAL AND NEW RISK CATEGORIES

The reinsurance industry is entering what Ernst & Young calls a "latent market demand" phase, where the traditional boundaries of the business are expanding in two critical directions: new types of risks to insure and new types of capital to finance that insurance.

THE CORE PROBLEM

Traditional reinsurance products have barely evolved in years. Cyber is the only major new line that has achieved real scale recently. Meanwhile, capacity in the market is up but demand is slightly down as primary insurers retain more risk themselves. This creates an awkward moment: there's more capital looking for returns, but fewer places to deploy it in traditional ways.

THE INNOVATION RESPONSE

Three things are happening simultaneously:

First, new risks are emerging faster than the industry can traditionally price them. AI development generates both infrastructure risks and novel operational risks that current insurance products weren't designed to handle. According to Aon, these emerging perils could present 37 percent higher maximum losses. This creates genuine demand for new financial structures, not just marketing.

Second, technology is making it possible to create those structures. Digital marketplaces, advanced analytics, and better pricing tools allow capital providers and risk-takers to find each other directly rather than relying on traditional broker relationships. This lowers friction and speeds up innovation cycles.

Third, alternative capital (now at a record $124 billion) has fundamentally changed the industry's structure. This isn't supplementary capital anymore—it's central. Private equity and other investors are willing to experiment with new vehicles like "AI-linked securities" (essentially catastrophe bonds tied to AI-related losses) and cyber bonds specifically because they're looking for differentiated returns.

WHY THIS MATTERS

The traditional reinsurer's competitive advantage is fragmenting. They can no longer win purely on scale or distribution relationships. Instead, the winning playbook involves either: specializing deeply in specific risk categories that alternative capital avoids, or becoming advisory partners who help sophisticated capital providers structure risk in ways that match their return objectives and exit timelines.

The mention of tokenization and digital currencies hints at a longer-term efficiency play—reducing foreign exchange costs and settlement friction in a market that moves enormous amounts of capital across borders.

This mirrors what happens in other mature financial markets when technology lowers barriers to entry: consolidation at the top, fragmentation in the middle, and a shift from product differentiation to service sophistication.

# Lagos State Parametric Flood Insurance: What's Actually Happening Here

Lagos just did something genuinely interesting with a $7.5 million parametric flood insurance policy. This deserves unpacking because it reveals how climate risk financing is evolving in the developing world, and what makes parametric insurance different from traditional coverage.

## The Basic Setup

Lagos State—a coastal megacity of 22 million people—is vulnerable to flooding that's getting worse due to climate change and rapid urbanization. About 80% of the population is low-income with almost no insurance. The government needed a way to get money quickly when floods hit, not years later after damage assessments.

So they bought a parametric policy. Here's the crucial distinction: traditional insurance pays based on actual losses you prove. Parametric insurance pays based on whether a trigger event occurred—in this case, if rainfall or flooding reaches a predetermined threshold. You don't wait for damage assessments. The money arrives based on the model saying "a flood of this magnitude happened."

## Why This Matters

This is economically sensible for several reasons:

First, it eliminates the assessment delay problem. In disaster zones, waiting six months for loss adjusters to determine damage is useless. You need capital immediately for rescue, medical care, and preventing secondary disasters. Parametric insurance solves that.

Second, it's cheaper to underwrite. Instead of arguing about individual losses, insurers price based on historical flood probability and severity models. Less dispute, lower administrative costs, wider availability.

Third, in a low-insurance environment like Lagos, parametric products are more scalable. You don't need detailed property registries and individual valuations. You just need good satellite data and historical flood models—which is precisely why ICEYE (a satellite firm) and JBA Risk Management (flood modelers) are involved.

## The Structural Reality

The ISF (InsuResilience Solutions Solutions Fund) financed 90% of the first year's premium. This is development finance, not commercial insurance. Lagos is committing to pay more of the premium in years two and three.

This reveals the actual mechanics: climate-vulnerable developing states can't afford market-rate insurance premiums for catastrophic risks. So multilateral development organizations subsidize the initial purchase to prove the model works and build government commitment. The hypothesis is that once embedded in fiscal planning, governments maintain it.

## What Could Actually Fail Here

Parametric insurance has a known problem: basis risk. The trigger might not perfectly correlate with actual losses. A model says "flood occurred" but your neighborhood didn't flood. You get paid anyway, which is fine, but the policy doesn't actually protect the specific people who suffered. This works well for government fiscal planning but imperfectly for individual resilience.

Also, these models require continuous recalibration. Climate change means historical patterns degrade. If flood probability shifts, the pricing that made sense in 2024 doesn't work in 2030.

## Why This Is News

This is noteworthy because it's a functional public-private mechanism for getting climate risk capital to places that need it. It's not perfect—the basis risk problem is real, and it's not clear this scales nationally in Nigeria—but it's substantially more pragmatic than most climate finance architecture, which tends to be either virtue signaling or perpetually stuck in planning.

The model is: identify vulnerable jurisdiction, build technical consortium (insurers plus modelers plus satellite firms), get development finance to subsidize initial premium, prove it works, build institutional commitment, transition to partial self-funding. That's actually a replicable playbook.

SUMMARY: GAM AND SWISS RE EXPAND INSURANCE-LINKED SECURITIES PARTNERSHIP

The basic story here is fairly straightforward but worth understanding if you care about how financial plumbing works in the catastrophe insurance space.

GAM Investments, a global asset manager, has formalized a partnership with Swiss Re (specifically Swiss Re's investment advisory arm SRILIAC) to jointly manage catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities funds. This is now "fully activated" as of 2025.

WHY THIS MATTERS

Insurance-linked securities are a way for insurance companies and reinsurers to transfer catastrophic risk to capital markets investors. Instead of keeping all the risk on their balance sheet, they can sell it to pension funds, hedge funds, and other investors looking for yield. This is basically securitizing insurance risk the way mortgages get securitized.

The partnership creates a few practical benefits:

First, liquidity. When you're managing multi-billion dollar pools of these assets, being able to buy and sell positions easily matters enormously. Swiss Re's involvement (they're literally one of the world's biggest reinsurers) presumably means better access to counterparties and tighter bid-ask spreads. This directly benefits investors in GAM's funds.

Second, expertise leverage. Swiss Re has actual underwriting knowledge about what risks are real versus what risks are being mispriced. GAM gets to tap into that. This is valuable because the people picking the securities should understand the underlying risks.

Third, product innovation. They're planning new ILS products for 2026. This matters because the ILS space historically has had relatively limited product variety compared to other alternatives.

THE BUSINESS MODEL ANGLE

This looks like a classic "we're big separately, we're more formidable together" arrangement. GAM gets Swiss Re's credibility and risk expertise. Swiss Re gets a distribution channel and can have its underwriting expertise embedded into investment products that will attract capital. Both benefit from scale - the combined multi-billion dollar AUM creates more liquidity, which attracts more capital, which creates a virtuous cycle.

For investors in these funds, the partnership should translate into slightly better returns (tighter dealing terms, better execution) and presumably lower risk (better underwriting). Whether that actually pans out depends on execution.

# Insurance-Linked Securities: Casualty Risk as the Next Frontier

The insurance-linked securities (ILS) market is experiencing a significant evolution. What started in the mid-1990s as primarily a mechanism for transferring catastrophic property risk is now expanding into casualty and liability risks, according to analysis from Cohen & Company Asset Management.

## The Setup

Think of ILS like this: Instead of insurers keeping all their risk on their balance sheets, they package it up and sell it to investors through securities. Historically, this worked well for property catastrophe—hurricanes in Florida, earthquakes in California. These are discrete, measurable events. The market for these instruments has grown to roughly $121 billion in alternative capital by mid-2025, driven by consistently strong returns and growing comfort with the structures.

## Why Casualty Risk is Different (and Why That Matters)

Casualty risks are "long-tail" exposures. Think workers' compensation claims or product liability—these play out over years or even decades, not instantaneous weather events. The cash flows are more predictable. They're also less sensitive to climate changes and macroeconomic shocks that drive traditional asset prices.

For investors, casualty ILS offers something genuinely valuable: returns that look more like private equity but with low correlation to stocks, bonds, and even existing catastrophe ILS. It's genuine diversification, not just a different pocket of the same risk.

## How It's Actually Happening

The real mechanism here is sidecars and quota shares. Imagine a reinsurer wants to write more casualty business but doesn't have the capital. Rather than borrow expensively, they create a sidecar—essentially a dedicated investment vehicle that provides collateralized reinsurance. QBE Re pulled in $550 million this way for their casualty sidecar in 2026. Investors get exposure to the underwriting spread; the reinsurer gets capital without dilution.

## The Maturation Story

What's changed isn't the underlying economics of casualty risk—that's been financeable for years. What's changed is the plumbing: better data, standardized documentation, clearer governance, and exit liquidity. These reduce friction costs significantly. Early transactions (workers' comp securitizations, motor liability deals) proved the concept. Now the market is standardizing around repeatable structures.

This matters because institutional capital is only interested when the structures are transparent, comparable, and tradeable. We're at that inflection point.

## The Real Momentum

Three things are converging: casualty insurance pricing is hardening (meaning better returns), carriers desperately need capital efficiency post-pandemic, and alternative capital overall is hitting records. When you stack those together, you get genuine demand, not just experimental interest.

The prediction from Cohen & Company is that casualty ILS moves from niche allocation to core portfolio piece—probably within the next several years—as early deals establish performance track records and the infrastructure matures.

# Hail Risk Escalating as a Major Insurance Threat

The insurance industry is confronting a fundamental shift in catastrophe risk. Hail, historically treated as a minor nuisance compared to hurricanes and tornadoes, is now generating losses comparable to major hurricanes. This matters because it forces a reassessment of how the entire risk transfer system—from primary insurers through reinsurers to catastrophe bond investors—prices and manages exposure.

## The Scale of the Problem

The numbers are striking. Over 43 million U.S. properties face moderate-to-high hail risk, representing $17.84 trillion in reconstruction value. In 2025 alone, there were 142 days with damaging hail (versus a 20-year average of 122), affecting over 600,000 homes and $177 billion in property value.

The modeling is particularly revealing. In extreme 1-in-500 year scenarios, hail drives roughly 80% of losses from all severe convective storms—about $58 billion of a $71 billion total. Even more moderate events that occur every few decades can produce ~$30 billion in losses, matching a major hurricane.

Geographic concentration amplifies this. Texas dominates with 235,000 impacted homes in 2025, especially in the Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Austin, and San Antonio corridor, which sits on $2.2 trillion in exposed value.

## Why This Matters

This represents a classic insurance industry problem: systemic mispricing of a growing risk. When perils shift from secondary status to primary drivers of loss, it typically means:

- Underwriting models need updating (many carriers may still be underpricing hail)
- Capital requirements increase, reducing industry capacity
- Homeowners in high-risk areas face sharper premium increases
- Reinsurers and catastrophe bond investors must recalibrate their exposure

The concentration in places like Texas also creates aggregation risk—a single storm can impact densely packed, high-value urban centers rather than dispersing losses across rural areas.

## Compounding Pressures

The report notes that hail frequency is increasing while property density in storm-prone regions is also rising. This is a double squeeze: more storms hitting more expensive properties. Texas's growth into suburban sprawl and apartment complexes means each hail event affects more structures, and those structures are costlier to repair.

Europe is experiencing similar dynamics, with severe convective storms generating up to €50 billion in economic losses since 2000, concentrated in Germany (€12.3B) and France (€7.8B).

## The Recovery Ecosystem Insight

The report emphasizes something often overlooked: accurate pricing and modeling only work if the entire system coordinates. Underwriters need property-level vulnerability data. Catastrophe modelers need to map tail risks. Claims teams need rapid weather verification to deploy resources efficiently. Rebuilding professionals need clear damage assessment.

When any part of this chain breaks down, recovery slows, costs spike, and communities suffer longer dislocation. The real issue isn't just pricing individual properties—it's ensuring the whole apparatus functions smoothly after impact.

PARTNERRE SHIFTS AWAY FROM LORENZ RE SIDECAR STRUCTURE

PartnerRe, a major Bermuda reinsurance company, is significantly reducing its use of Lorenz Re, a special purpose vehicle it created in 2013 to manage third-party investor capital. This shift reveals how large reinsurers are adapting their strategies for accessing outside investment.

THE NUMBERS TELL THE STORY

The decline is dramatic. In 2022, PartnerRe ceded $664 million in written premiums to Lorenz Re. By 2024, that dropped to $392 million. In 2025, it fell to just $155 million—a 60 percent reduction in a single year.

The same pattern appears in PartnerRe's accounting for reinsurance recoverable amounts (essentially the outstanding risk exposure). This metric was $921 million at the end of 2022 but shrank to $445 million by December 2025.

WHY THIS MATTERS

The shift illustrates a broader evolution in how major reinsurers package their underwriting returns for outside investors. The Lorenz Re structure was essentially a private quota share arrangement—investors took a slice of PartnerRe's underwriting profits in exchange for capital. This worked for sophisticated allocators, but had limitations.

WHAT'S REPLACING IT

PartnerRe is now deploying multiple structures instead of relying on one vehicle. The Huygens sidecar has attracted increased allocations from major Dutch pension investor PGGM. More significantly, PartnerRe launched the PartnerRe ILS Fund, a traditional fund structure that appeals to broader allocator bases than private quota shares.

The fund approach is strategically smarter. It lets more types of investors participate without requiring deep relationships with individual portfolio companies. It's like the difference between a private investment and a mutual fund—both access the same returns, but the fund reaches vastly more capital sources.

This represents PartnerRe optimizing its third-party capital strategy by recognizing that one structure cannot efficiently serve all investor types.

# ZURICH RETURNS TO CAT BOND MARKET AFTER 13-YEAR ABSENCE

## The Basic Story

Zurich Insurance is coming back to the catastrophe bond market for the first time since 2012. They're issuing $125 million in bonds through a Bermuda-based vehicle called Turicum Re Ltd. to get reinsurance protection against US storms and earthquakes.

## Why This Matters

Think of catastrophe bonds as insurance-backed securities. When a major hurricane or earthquake hits, the bondholder absorbs some of the losses instead of traditional reinsurers. It's a way to spread risk across capital markets investors rather than keeping it concentrated with reinsurance companies.

Zurich's return signals something important: after years of skepticism about cat bonds as a risk management tool, major insurance players are deciding they're actually useful. The company already has traditional reinsurance coverage but is deliberately adding cat bonds on top. That's not desperation—that's strategic stacking.

## The Specific Deal Structure

The $125 million Class A tranche sits in a specific risk layer. It only triggers if losses hit $650 million and then covers claims up to $850 million. In cat bond language, it has a 9.22% probability of being triggered and an expected loss of 7.88%. The company is offering investors roughly 16.75-17.25% spread over risk-free rates.

These numbers are on the higher end for cat bonds, which makes sense—higher risk commands higher compensation.

## Why Now

The cat bond market has become more efficient and attractive on price. Multi-year coverage (this deal runs three years) gives Zurich predictable protection. By diversifying where they get reinsurance capital from—traditional reinsurers, capital markets, pooled arrangements—they're building resilience into their risk management structure.

It's a practical signal that after years of debate, cat bonds have matured into a legitimate part of how sophisticated insurers manage catastrophe risk.
